It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the “unsearchable riches” of Christ while the “noise and tumult” of heavy trials seeks to drown out the “spotless purity of truth,” and I must ask you with a gentle heart: why do you ask after the nature of perseverance in ministry and the weight of your afflictions? [11, 28, 1503, 1605, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling “overwhelmed and desperate” because your “labor of my hands” seems to meet only with “desolation,” or are you seeking a “settled certainty” to anchor your soul in the truth that the Master “sovereignly orders everything He has made”—including the “horrible pit” of your current suffering? [13, 20, 32, 1143, 1263, 1440, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many “shave off the edges” of the truth to offer “spiritual placebos” that ignore the reality of the cross, we must return to the “external Word” to see how the Lord personally provides for the “repose of the soul” by using trials to “perfect, confirm, strengthen and establish” His servants [11, 28, 136, 1503, 1515, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition—echoed by **John Calvin** and **Charles Spurgeon**—teaches that “God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation,” and therefore, your suffering is not an “administrative anomaly” but is subject to the “decree from God” who “works all things according to the counsel of His own will” [15, 68, 364, 379, 1143, 1532, 1637, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 1: God’s Absolute Sovereignty Over Your Affliction**

**Verse**
“ ‘Remember the former things of old, For I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like Me, Declaring the end from the beginning, And from ancient times things that are not yet done, Saying, “My counsel shall stand, And I will do all My pleasure” ’ ” (Isaiah 46:9–10). [1429, 1565, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Scripture reveals that time is a “one continuous plan of redemption” in which God “positively ordains whatsoever comes to pass” [1032, 1406, 1565, Conversation History]. Because God is the “Alpha and the Omega,” He “harnesses the deeds of the wicked” to accomplish His good ends, for “we know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are the called according to His purpose” (Romans 8:28; Revelation 1:8) [661, 825, 1032, 1566, 1567, Conversation History]. Even the “worst atrocity ever carried out”—the crucifixion of Christ—was subject to the “determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God,” proving that “nothing thwarts any aspect of His plan” (Acts 2:23) [5, 1132, 1431, 1567, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “trade in your worry for trust,” recognizing that “the Lord has established His throne in heaven, and His kingdom rules over all” (Psalm 103:19) [15, 94, 152, 201, 1143, 1408, 1515, Conversation History]. Confess your “insufficiency” and rest in the fact that “He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6) [5, 829, 1408, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Jewish vs. Gentile Context**
In the ancient **theocratic context**, “national prosperity” and having “large and beautiful cities” were often seen as “temporal signs” of God’s favor [409, 1353, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** this by showing that the “church militant” is an “assembly of the citizens of heaven” whose “inheritance is incorruptible,” for “Jesus answered, ‘My kingdom is not of this world’ ” (John 18:36; 1 Peter 1:4) [13, 26, 142, 830, 1313, 1426, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: Finding Strength While Preaching Through Pain**

**Verse**
“And He said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness.’ Therefore most gladly I will rather boast in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me” (2 Corinthians 12:9). [165, 841, 1207, 1209, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed faith teaches that suffering is “a way for God to display His grace and power,” and therefore a preacher should not seek “deliverance” from his “scars” but rather allow them to manifest the life of Jesus [843, Conversation History]. When you are “perplexed, but not in despair” and “persecuted, but not forsaken,” you carry “in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our body” (2 Corinthians 4:8–10) [980, 1067, 1403, Conversation History]. The Master allows a “thorn in the flesh” to ensure His servants are “not exalted above measure,” forcing them to rely “solely and only by His revealed truth” rather than their own “excellence of speech” (1 Corinthians 2:1; 2 Corinthians 12:7) [19, 989, 1316, 1513, 1529, 1587, 1646, 1720, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Wait for His Son from heaven” and find “tranquility of soul” in the promise that “your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58; 1 Thessalonians 1:10) [24, 101, 192, 198, 201, 483, 853, 1315, 1408, 1515, 1670, Conversation History]. Recognize that “your life is not your own” but is “hid with Christ in God,” so you can “take pleasure in infirmities... for Christ’s sake” (2 Corinthians 12:10; Colossians 3:3) [12, 101, 841, 1138, 1262, 1406, 1670, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: From Ritual to Reality**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, “animal sacrifices” were a “shadow” that required physical perfection [11, 402, 1313, 1430, 1442, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “spiritual service of worship,” showing that God values the “broken and a contrite heart” and the “living sacrifice” of a body that endures “various trials” for His name (Psalm 51:17; Romans 12:1; James 1:2) [17, 36, 163, 852, 861, 940, 1152, 1235, 1406, 1503, 1515, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: The Duty to Endure as a Good Soldier**

**Verse**
“You therefore must endure hardship as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. No one engaged in warfare entangles himself with the affairs of this life, that he may please him who enlisted him as a soldier” (2 Timothy 2:3–4). [1167, 1202, 1204, 1458, 1642, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Perseverance in ministry is a “disciplined life” where the “faithful slave” is “loyal and submissive” to the King despite “noise and tumult” [12, 13, 20, 31, 121, 130, 212, 1138, 1262, 1406, 1605, 1670, Conversation History]. Because “salvation is a supernatural work of God,” those who are “truly born again will be kept by God’s power and will persevere as Christians until the end of their lives” [333, 472, Conversation History]. We are called to “contend earnestly for the faith” without being “pugnacious or quarrelsome,” for “a servant of the Lord must not quarrel but be gentle to all, able to teach, patient” (2 Timothy 2:24; Jude 3) [81, 1514, 1515, 1572, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You must “discipline your body and bring it into subjection,” refusing to “lose heart” because “the Judge is standing at the door!” (1 Corinthians 9:27; James 5:9) [79, 116, 280, 312, 1203, 1315, 1406, 1709, Conversation History]. “Saturate and renew your mind” with the truth that “the Word of our God stands forever,” even when your “flesh and my heart fail” (Psalm 73:26; Isaiah 40:8) [11, 105, 116, 121, 1071, 1175, 1179, 1306, 1406, 1684, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Revision of Warfare**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, God used “the sword” as a “temporal sign” of His “fierce anger” [395, 668, 717, 1110, 1316, 1353, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “victory,” teaching that we “conquer” not through “carnal weaponry” but “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11) [13, 21, 32, 92, 1113, 1210, 1313, 1402, 1491, 1515, 1646, 1670, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 4: The Settled Certainty of God’s Keeping Power**

**Verse**
“Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling, and to make you stand in the presence of His glory blameless with great joy, to the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen” (Jude 24–25). [473, 1533, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed tradition asserts that the “firm foundation of God stands,” having the “seal” that “The Lord knows those who are His” (2 Timothy 2:19) [11, 147, 176, 300, 361, 413, 1138, 1450, Conversation History]. Our perseverance does not depend on our “amazing energy, skill, and focus,” but on the fact that “God is able to keep you from stumbling,” for “His understanding is infinite” (Psalm 147:5) [102, 244, 473, 835, 1193, 1352, Conversation History]. We are “protected by the power of God” through a “faith” that is “not your own” but a “saving grace, wrought in the heart of a sinner by the Spirit and Word of God” (1 Peter 1:5) [230, 442, 473, 1515, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Wait for His Son from heaven,” knowing that “perfect justice will come” and He will “wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:10) [14, 24, 94, 109, 201, 470, 816, 822, 948, 1315, 1408, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History]. Find “repose of the soul” in Christ’s “finished work,” recognizing that “death is but a harmless shadow for the sheep of the Good Shepherd” (John 19:30) [13, 24, 142, 198, 844, 1016, 1313, 1426, 1445, Conversation History].

***

**Final Reminder**
“Nevertheless the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness’ ” (2 Timothy 2:19). [11, 147, 176, 211, 222, 285, 300, 361, 405, 414, 444, 591, 1138, 1450, Conversation History].

references.cited_text: If we would prevail, we must persist; we must continue incessantly and constantly, and know no pause to our prayer till we win the mercy to the fullest possible extent. “Men ought always to pray.” Week by week, month by month, year by year; the conversion of that dear child is to be the father’s main plea. The bringing in of that unconverted husband is to lie upon the wife’s heart night and day till she gets it; she is not to take even ten or twenty years of unsuccessful prayer as a reason why she should cease; she is to set God no times nor seasons, but so long as there is life in her and life in the dear object of her solicitude, she is to continue still to plead with the mighty God of Jacob. The pastor is not to seek a blessing on his people occasionally, and then in receiving a measure of it to desist from further intercession, but he is to continue vehemently without pause, without restraining his energies, to cry aloud and spare not till the windows of heaven be opened and a blessing be given too large for him to house. But, brethren, how many times we ask of God, and have not because we do not wait long enough at the door! We knock a time or two at the gate of mercy, and as no friendly messenger opens the door, we go our ways. Too many prayers are like boys’ runaway knocks, given, and then the giver is away before the door can be opened. O for grace to stand foot to foot with the angel of God, and never, never, never relax our hold; feeling that the cause we plead is one in which we must be successful, for souls depend on it, the glory of God is connected with it, the state of our fellow men is in jeopardy. If we could have given up in prayer our own lives and the lives of those dearest to us, yet the souls of men we cannot give up, we must urge and plead again and again until we obtain the answer.3

He is capable of doing all Khayyám wrote about and more, but the balancing factor is that God cares about us. We will soon explore that truth in more detail. In Scripture, the mighty hand of God’s power means different things at different times. Sometimes it speaks of deliverance, as in the exodus of Israel from Egypt (Ex. 3:20). Sometimes it serves as a shield to protect the believer through a time of testing. Sometimes it is a chastening hand.

The Shallow Hearer The soil spread thinly over a layer of rock illustrates a shallow-hearted person who responds immediately but only superficially. “The ones on the rock are those who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, who believe for a while and in time of temptation fall away” (Luke 8:13). Without deep roots, vegetation cannot live long in a dry climate. It grows green and leafy quickly, but dies just as quickly, before reaching fruit-bearing maturity. Such growth is useless for any profitable purpose.

All three varieties of fruitless soil are emblematic of unbelievers—including those who originally showed some promise but failed to bear fruit. The Fruitful Hearer The final soil is well cultivated and produces the desired crop. Jesus says this symbolizes “those who, having heard the word with a noble and good heart, keep it and bear fruit with patience” (Luke 8:15). This is the truly prepared heart. In Matthew 13:23, Jesus says the good soil pictures a person “who hears the word and understands it.” In Mark 4:20, He says it is a symbol of “those who hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit” (emphasis added).

The master’s response shows him to be a gracious and generous man. He rewarded the faithful stewards with expanded authority, increased opportunity, and a place of joy and favor. Their reward clearly pictures heaven. Heaven is not a place of eternal boredom and tedious inactivity; it is filled with exaltation and honor, expanded opportunities for service, and the greatest joy of all—endless fellowship with Christ Himself. The promises and parables of Jesus are full of similar imagery signifying heaven (cf. Luke 12:35–37, 44; 19:17–19; 22:29–30; John 12:26).

No miracle of any magnitude will convince someone who hears and understands the message of Scripture but rejects it anyway. Only the Holy Spirit can open blind eyes and melt hardened hearts to receive the Word. And the truth of God’s Word is the only message with the power to save. If you reject the Word of God but believe in some miracle, religious experience, or private revelation, your faith is not saving faith at all. And those the Word of God will be judged by the very truth they reject. In John 12:46–48 Jesus said, “I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes in Me should not abide in darkness. And if anyone hears My words and does not believe, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world. He who rejects Me, and does not receive My words, has that which judges him—the word that I have spoken will judge him in the last day.”

To them, the terrifying weight of Christ’s question, “Why do you call Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46) directly applies.
